title: Short Stuff: Pie-In-The-Face Gag
summary: Short Stuff episode on the pie-in-the-face comedy gag. The hosts trace its origins to vaudeville in the late 1800s with Canadian performer Doc Kelly, then its spread into silent films starting with the possibly lost 1909 film Mister Flip (starring Ben Turpin) and the 1913 Keystone film The Noise from the Deep (Mabel Normand, Fatty Arbuckle), with Keystone Studios baking its own pies. They cover the 1916 Charlie Chaplin film Behind the Screen parodying the gag, Laurel and Hardy's 1927 Battle of the Century (about 4,500 pies), Buster Keaton's rules for the bit (don't turn too early and flinch, pies should be brittle with double crust, shaving cream replacing real filling), the spoiled pies on The Great Race (1963/64), star pie throwers like Fatty Arbuckle and Moe Howard, and real-life pieing of public figures such as Thomas Forcade, Bill Gates and Rupert Murdoch by the Biotic Baking Brigade. Ends with a break and sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Short Stuff episode, with Chuck and Jerry standing in for Dave, and names the topic of the pie-in-the-face gag.

segments.title: Origins in vaudeville with Doc Kelly
segments.summary: The hosts describe why the pie-in-the-face gag works comically and credit Canadian vaudeville performer Doc Kelly with popularizing it after seeing a cook throw pie at a stable boy, saying it should hit the face instead.

segments.title: Early silent films: Mister Flip and The Noise from the Deep
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the 1909 Ben Turpin film Mister Flip, which is lost and known only from descriptions, and the 1913 Keystone film The Noise from the Deep with Mabel Normand and Fatty Arbuckle, the earliest documented pie gag, noting Keystone's in-house bakery.

segments.title: Overuse, Behind the Screen and Battle of the Century
segments.summary: The gag became overdone by 1916, parodied in Charlie Chaplin's Behind the Screen. It returned in 1927 with Laurel and Hardy's Battle of the Century, which used a huge number of pies.

segments.title: Battle of the Century pie order and rediscovered footage
segments.summary: The hosts say Battle of the Century started with 4,500 pies from the Los Angeles Pie Company, that the current edited version is weaker than the original, and that some original footage was reportedly found in a basement, possibly at USC.

segments.title: Later pie gag and Buster Keaton's rules; pie construction
segments.summary: The gag lived on with Little Rascals and Three Stooges. Buster Keaton's unwritten rules: the target should deserve it, often a snooty high-society figure. Pies were baked to brittleness with a double crust so they shatter without cutting the face, and not served in tin plates.

segments.title: Fake pies and cheap versions
segments.summary: The hosts discuss spoof pies made from a tin with whipped cream or shaving cream and no filling, contrasted with real pies, and Josh recalls a childhood pie-in-the-face party using Cool Whip.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: The hosts take a break before returning.

segments.title: Transition after break
segments.summary: Brief audio transition back into the episode with the hosts' sound cues.

segments.title: Keaton's flinching rule, filling choices, and The Great Race
segments.summary: Keaton warned against turning too early because flinching forces reshoots. Blonde hair and light fillings worked best on black-and-white film. Shaving cream replaced real filling because it doesn't spoil. In The Great Race (1963 or 1964), pies left out over Memorial Day weekend spoiled, leading to shaving cream.

segments.title: Pie-throwing champions: Fatty Arbuckle and Moe Howard
segments.summary: Some performers were known as champion pie throwers. Fatty Arbuckle could reportedly throw one with each hand, and Moe Howard of the Three Stooges did off-camera throwing and was hired out for other films.

segments.title: Real-life pieing of public figures and the Biotic Baking Brigade
segments.summary: The gag moved into real life as activists pied powerful people such as Bill Gates and Rupert Murdoch. Thomas Forcade, founder of High Times, was said to be the first. The Biotic Baking Brigade of San Francisco pied targets like neo-Nazis, Klansmen and homophobic preachers.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wrap up the Short Stuff segment, with the standard iHeartRadio production credit.
